svg.title: Common supply-chain attacks, and where Smarter stops them
svg.desc: Eight common supply-chain attacks, numbered where each enters Smarter's pipeline, from upstream maintainers, through the registries, the build and the release, to the running platform, with the control that stops or reduces each one. 1, typosquatting, a look-alike package name: every name enters through a reviewed lockfile change; reduced. 2, dependency confusion: one public index, exact versions and hashes; blocked. 3, a maintainer's account taken over to publish a malicious release: exact pins, a 14-day cooldown on new releases and pip-audit; reduced. 4, a tampered artifact, replaced on the registry or in transit: pip installs with require-hashes; blocked. 5, a hijacked CI action, a tag moved to a malicious commit: actions are pinned to commit SHAs; blocked. 6, a poisoned base image: the official Python image with OS updates at each build, and ECR scanning; reduced. 7, a swapped release: Cosign signatures, an SBOM and SLSA provenance, deployed by verified digest; blocked. 8, a malicious plugin or extension, third-party code that answers tool calls: the signed registry names the publisher, and the tool worker runs its code with no credentials, no database and no private addresses; reduced.
svg.text: Common supply-chain attacks, and where Smarter stops them
each numbered attack enters at one stage of the pipeline; the card below it names Smarter's control
The pipeline an attack must travel
is uploaded, waiting for someone's typo.
Every package name enters through a lockfile
change in a public, reviewed pull request.
A public package takes the name of a private
one, with a higher version, and wins the install.
One public index and no private names; exact
versions and file hashes, so no index can swap one.
A stolen login or token publishes a malicious
release of a real, trusted package.
Exact pins; a 14-day cooldown on new releases
A release's file is replaced on the registry,
or altered on its way to the build.
pip install --require-hashes: a file whose sha256
isn't the lockfile's fails the build.
An action's tag (v4) is moved to a malicious
commit that runs in the release pipeline.
Every GitHub Action is pinned to a commit SHA,
and updated by Dependabot after two weeks.
The OS image the build starts from carries
a backdoor or a vulnerable package.
Official Python image, from ECR Public; OS updates
at each build; ECR scans every pushed image.
A different image or chart is pushed under
the release's tag, to registries or mirrors.
Cosign signatures in Sigstore's public log, an SBOM
and SLSA provenance; deploy by verified digest.
Third-party code is installed at run time and
runs to answer the LLM's tool calls.
A signed registry names the publisher; the tool
worker runs its code with no credentials or database.
An attack that gets through runs inside the application, with the platform's own permissions.
